corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'outperform Arrays.binarySearch by up to 25% on Oracle JDK, up to 16% on GraalVM on Apple M4 ARM64 (Neon 128-bit)' and 'up to 24% on Oracle JDK, up to 29% on GraalVM on x86-64 AMD (AVX2 256-bit)'; 'p99 values are better than default binary search almost in all test cases'. The percentages are reductions in mean ns/op of simdQuadSearch versus binarySearchDefault and match the best single result files: arm64 Oracle 4k warm 32.540 vs 24.496 ns/op (24.7%), arm64 GraalVM 64k cold 240.503 vs 201.196 (16.3%), amd64 Oracle 16k warm 202.130 vs 153.170 (24.2%), amd64 GraalVM 8k cold 659.617 vs 466.574 (29.3%, about 1.41x) (derived from page data). docs/results/amd64 Oracle JDK 1m cold: binarySearchDefault 1192.757 ns/op, quadSearch 1020.096 ns/op, simdQuadSearch 1053.785 ns/op (about 12% less time for the SIMD variant, derived from page data). Typical gains across the 72 files are 5 to 15%.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Java 25 toolchain (Oracle JDK and GraalVM; exact builds not stated), JMH 1.37 via the me.champeau.jmh 0.7.3 Gradle plugin, Mode.SampleTime, 3 forks, 5 x 2 s warmup, 10 x 2 s measurement; JVM args --add-modules=jdk.incubator.vector --enable-preview -Xms12g -Xmx12g -XX:+UseG1GC (build.gradle); run-benchmarks.sh sweeps the nine sizes for both benchmarks
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 (arm64, NEON 128-bit) and an unnamed x86-64 AMD CPU with AVX2 (model not stated in the README, the results files or docs/index.html)
corrections.workload: Quaternary narrowing over 16-element block boundaries, then a Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector, SPECIES_PREFERRED) block scan, versus Arrays.binarySearch over sorted, strictly increasing int arrays of 4k to 1m elements (array count shrinks from 256k to 1k as size grows, about 4 GB of data per run). Cold-cache runs switch arrays on every query; warm-cache runs reuse each array for 128 consecutive queries (README says 100). Queries are uniform in [0, 8n) while array values average 4.5n, so about 44% of queries lie beyond the last element. JMH sample mode on Oracle JDK and GraalVM.

notes: Numbers, sizes and README percentages all check out against docs/results; the search code keeps Arrays.binarySearch return semantics and looks correct. The record's caveat that the gain comes mostly from quaternary narrowing holds on amd64 only: on arm64 the non-SIMD quadSearch is slower than binarySearch at 4k to 16k cold (up to 18% slower) and the SIMD scan carries the win; simdQuadSearch is itself slower than binarySearch in amd64 GraalVM 16k warm (206.206 vs 197.172 ns/op) and arm64 GraalVM 4k warm (34.412 vs 33.388), and p99 is worse in a few cells. Java-only project (Vector API incubator, --enable-preview), 3 stars, 12 commits, no releases.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go version for the README runs not stated (go.mod declares go 1.18; CI uses Go 1.25); assembly generated from C by gocc (clang) with -O3 and --arch avx2 / neon / apple per codegen/generate.sh; default go test -bench settings; the SPEEDUP column is base-mode ns/op divided by simd-mode ns/op from runBenchmark in simd_test.go
corrections.workload: Element-wise add/sub/mul/div and sum/min/max reductions on uint8..uint64, int8..int64, float32 and float64 slices of 256, 4096 and 16384 elements filled with the repeating pattern (i % 100) + 1; the baseline is the package's own generic scalar Go loop (selected by setting hardware=false), the fast path is clang auto-vectorized C translated to Plan9 assembly (AVX2 on amd64, NEON on arm64).
corrections.caveats: Many rows exceed 50x (uint16 min 16384 84.12x, int8 min/max 16384 about 68.7x on the i7-13700K; uint8 max 4096 65.16x on the M3 Pro) against a hand-written scalar Go loop, not slices.Min or the min/max builtins; Go's compiler does not auto-vectorize, so the ratio mostly measures clang vectorization versus scalar Go, on L1/L2-resident data. Division gives about 1x and is slower in several rows (uint16 div 16384 0.79x, int8 div 0.69x to 0.71x on the i7-13700K). The SIMD path takes &input[0] without length checks, so an empty slice panics, and Add/Sub/Mul/Div pass len(dst) to the assembly without checking input1/input2, so shorter inputs are read out of bounds. Capped at C because the Go version is not stated.

notes: All seven claimed figures appear verbatim in the README i7-13700K table; the README tables were regenerated in the 2026-03-07 commit (15bded0) together with the assembly. Baseline is the library's own scalar fallback, which matches the category's 'scalar reference' baseline only loosely (Go, not C/C++). corrections.caveats: The README itself says that as of .NET 9 the library is mostly unnecessary because the runtime LINQ received most of these optimizations; the baseline is .NET Framework 4.x LINQ, which is far slower than modern .NET LINQ. The benchmark methods for these rows are commented out in Benchmarks/Benchmarks.cs at HEAD and TEST_SIZE there is 1000000 (data i % 2), so the published 100000-element run is not reproducible as checked in. SumS (SIMD) sums without overflow checking while LINQ Sum on int throws OverflowException, so the 55x Sum row compares unequal semantics; OrderByF is not a stable sort while LINQ OrderBy is (README Limitations). Several ratios exceed 50x (Sum SIMD about 55.4x, derived). Library code unchanged since 2019-07-12; the 2025-09-26 commit only edited the README.
